title: Crime emergency declared in the District of Columbia and Metropolitan Police placed under Federal control
whatHappened: Executive Order 14333 declared a crime emergency in the District of Columbia, invoked section 740 of the District of Columbia Home Rule Act to place the Metropolitan Police Department under Federal control, and directed the Secretary of Defense to provide National Guard support. Executive Orders 14339 and 14340 of 25 August 2025 extended the measures.
whatItChanged: Placed the capital's police force under direct Federal command and put National Guard personnel on the streets of Washington; the template was reused in Memphis and Illinois within eight weeks.
sourceName: Executive Order 14333, Declaring a Crime Emergency in the District of Columbia (Federal Register)

title: Lethal military strike campaign begun against designated drug-trafficking organisations in the Caribbean Sea and Eastern Pacific Ocean
whatHappened: The statutory report to Congress on the legal and policy frameworks for the use of military force records that 'Since September 2025, the United States military has conducted precision strikes against violent drug trafficking organizations that have been designated as terrorist organizations' in the Caribbean Sea and Eastern Pacific Ocean, ordered under claimed Article II authority and the inherent right of self-defence. The same report lists the Caribbean Sea and Eastern Pacific Ocean among the regions where force was used in calendar year 2025. NOTE: this openable primary dates the campaign only to 'September 2025'; the date field is set to the first of that month and the exact first-strike date is not established here from a primary source.
whatItChanged: Opened a standing lethal military campaign in the Western Hemisphere against non-state trafficking targets outside any congressional authorisation for the use of military force, and supplied the legal predicate later invoked for the operation in Venezuela.
sourceName: The White House, Report on the Legal and Policy Frameworks for the United States' Use of Military Force and Related National Security Operations (50 U.S.C. 1549(a), calendar year 2025)

title: Department of Defense redesignated the Department of War
whatHappened: Executive Order 14347 directed that 'Department of War' be used as a secondary title for the Department of Defense and that 'Secretary of War' be used for the Secretary of Defense, and directed the Secretary to recommend legislative and executive actions to make the renaming permanent.
whatItChanged: Changed the name under which the United States military establishment issues orders, publishes and is addressed in law; official communications and the department's public web presence moved to the War Department identity.
sourceName: Executive Order 14347, Restoring the United States Department of War (Federal Register)

title: Charlie Kirk assassinated at Utah Valley University
whatHappened: Charlie Kirk was shot and killed by a single rifle round fired from a rooftop while speaking at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) took part in the manhunt; Tyler Robinson was taken into custody on 11 September 2025 and a bolt-action rifle was recovered near the campus.
whatItChanged: Killed the founder of a major national political organisation in front of a public audience; the President ordered flags to half-staff by proclamation the same day.
sourceName: Federal Bureau of Investigation, Utah Valley Shooting Updates

title: Memphis Safe Task Force established and National Guard directed to Memphis
whatHappened: A Presidential Memorandum established the Memphis Safe Task Force and directed the Secretary of War to request that the Governor of Tennessee make Tennessee National Guard units available for public safety and law enforcement support in Memphis, and to coordinate with other State Governors to mobilise additional National Guard personnel.
whatItChanged: Extended the District of Columbia deployment model to a State city, with the Guard operating under State control at Federal request.
sourceName: The White House, Presidential Memorandum: Restoring Law and Order in Memphis

title: Entry of H-1B specialty occupation workers restricted absent a $100,000 payment
whatHappened: A Presidential Proclamation restricted entry of aliens as nonimmigrants under section 101(a)(15)(H)(i)(b) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) except where the petition is accompanied by a payment of $100,000, effective 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on 21 September 2025 and expiring, absent extension, twelve months later. The Secretary of Homeland Security was directed to restrict decisions on petitions not accompanied by the payment.
whatItChanged: Imposed a six-figure per-petition charge on the principal skilled-worker visa route and suspended entry for petitions without it.
sourceName: Proclamation, Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers (Federal Register)

title: Forty-three-day lapse in appropriations, the longest in United States history
whatHappened: Appropriations lapsed on 1 October 2025 and the funding gap ran forty-three days. It ended on 12 November 2025 with the enactment of the Continuing Appropriations, Agriculture, Legislative Branch, Military Construction and Veterans Affairs, and Extensions Act, 2026 (Public Law 119-37), which provided full-year appropriations for three bills and a continuing resolution for the rest of the government.
whatItChanged: Suspended most non-excepted Federal operations for six weeks and left the remaining appropriations bills on a short fuse that produced two further shutdowns within three months.
sourceName: Public Law 119-37, Continuing Appropriations, Agriculture, Legislative Branch, Military Construction and Veterans Affairs, and Extensions Act, 2026 (govinfo)

title: Illinois National Guard called into Federal service over the Governor's objection
whatHappened: A Presidential Memorandum invoked 10 U.S.C. 12406 to call at least 300 members of the Illinois National Guard into Federal service 'until the Governor of Illinois consents to a federally-funded mobilization' under Title 32, to protect Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Federal Protective Service (FPS) and other Federal personnel and property in Illinois.
whatItChanged: Federalised a State's National Guard against the express position of its Governor, moving the domestic deployment question from cooperative request to compelled Federal service.
sourceName: The White House, Presidential Memorandum: Department of War Security for the Protection of Federal Personnel and Property in Illinois

title: Nationwide 'No Kings' day of protest
whatHappened: UNRESOLVED. Coordinated single-day demonstrations were reported in some 2,700 cities and towns across all fifty States, with organiser and advocacy-group estimates of roughly seven million participants, the largest single-day protest count reported in the United States. No government statement, legislative research-service product, court ruling or official gazette establishing the event or any participation figure could be opened; the only sources located were news outlets and participating advocacy organisations, which the source rule excludes. Pass A should attempt a targeted primary (for example a congressional floor record or a municipal police after-action report) before any downstream pass relies on this.
whatItChanged: Not established from a primary source.
sourceName: UNRESOLVED — no primary source located

title: California Proposition 50 approved, replacing commission-drawn congressional maps through 2030
whatHappened: At the 4 November 2025 Statewide Special Election, California voters approved Proposition 50, which requires legislatively drawn congressional district maps passed in August 2025 to be used through 2030 in place of the maps drawn by the California Citizens Redistricting Commission. The Secretary of State published certified results by congressional district.
whatItChanged: Converted the country's largest congressional delegation to legislature-drawn maps for the remainder of the decade, in an explicit mid-decade response to Texas's redistricting.
sourceName: California Secretary of State, Statement of Vote, 2025 Statewide Special Election — Proposition 50 Results by Congressional District

title: Full pardons granted for offences related to the 2020 presidential election
whatHappened: A Presidential Proclamation granted full, complete and unconditional pardons for offences relating to efforts to contest or alter the outcome of the 2020 presidential election, covering a schedule of named individuals.
whatItChanged: Extinguished Federal criminal exposure for a defined class of participants in the post-2020 election challenges.
sourceName: Proclamation, Granting Pardons for Certain Offenses Related to the 2020 Presidential Election (Federal Register)

title: Epstein Files Transparency Act enacted
whatHappened: Public Law 119-38 (H.R. 4405) required the Attorney General, within thirty days, to make publicly available in searchable and downloadable form all unclassified records in the possession of the Department of Justice, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation and United States Attorneys' Offices, relating to Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell, including flight logs, named individuals and entities, and immunity, non-prosecution and plea agreements.
whatItChanged: Statutorily compelled disclosure of an entire Federal investigative file over the executive branch's stated preference, and set the deadline that produced the January 2026 release.
sourceName: Public Law 119-38, Epstein Files Transparency Act (govinfo)

title: Muslim Brotherhood chapters designated Foreign Terrorist Organizations
whatHappened: Executive Order 14362 directed the Secretary of State and the Secretary of the Treasury to designate certain chapters of the Muslim Brotherhood as Foreign Terrorist Organizations (FTOs) and Specially Designated Global Terrorists (SDGTs), and to report on the designations within specified deadlines.
whatItChanged: Extended terrorism designation authority to chapters of a transnational political-religious movement, with the criminal material-support and sanctions consequences that follow designation.
sourceName: Executive Order 14362, Designation of Certain Muslim Brotherhood Chapters as Foreign Terrorist Organizations and Specially Designated Global Terrorists (Federal Register)

title: National Guard members ambushed near the White House; Specialist Sarah Beckstrom killed
whatHappened: At about 2:13 p.m. on 26 November 2025, at 17th and I Streets NW near the Farragut West Metro station, Rahmanullah Lakanwal opened fire on National Guard members deployed in Washington. Specialist Sarah Beckstrom of the West Virginia Army National Guard was killed and Sergeant Andrew Wolfe was seriously injured. Federal charges including first degree murder while armed were brought and a superseding indictment followed.
whatItChanged: Killed a Guard member deployed under the capital crime-emergency mission; the President ordered flags to half-staff by proclamation on 4 December 2025, and an expanded entry restriction on foreign nationals followed on 16 December 2025.
sourceName: United States Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia, Afghan National Charged with the Murder of National Guard Soldier Sarah Beckstrom

title: Entry of foreign nationals restricted and limited on security grounds
whatHappened: A Presidential Proclamation restricted and limited the entry of foreign nationals into the United States, expanding the country-based suspension and limitation of entry in place since 2025.
whatItChanged: Widened the set of nationalities barred or limited from entry, three weeks after the Washington Guard ambush.
sourceName: Proclamation, Restricting and Limiting the Entry of Foreign Nationals To Protect the Security of the United States (Federal Register)

title: Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act enacted, repealing the 2002 Iraq force authorisation
whatHappened: Public Law 119-60, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, was signed on 18 December 2025. The statutory report to Congress on the legal frameworks for the use of military force records that section 8370 of the Act repealed the 2002 Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq (Public Law 107-243), and that United States forces continued operating in Iraq and Syria under the 2001 Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF).
whatItChanged: Removed one of the two standing statutory war authorisations, leaving the 2001 AUMF and claimed Article II authority as the basis for ongoing operations.
sourceName: Public Law 119-60, National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (govinfo)

title: Enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits lapsed
whatHappened: The enhanced premium tax credit schedule under section 36B of the Internal Revenue Code, extended by section 12001 of Public Law 117-169, applies to taxable years 'after December 31, 2020, and before January 1, 2026'. No extension was enacted before that date, so the enhanced schedule and the removal of the 400-percent-of-poverty income cap lapsed at the end of 2025.
whatItChanged: Raised net marketplace premiums for subsidised enrollees from plan year 2026 and removed subsidy eligibility above 400 percent of the poverty line; extension of these credits was the central demand in the October-November 2025 shutdown.
sourceName: Public Law 117-169, section 12001 (Improve Affordability and Reduce Premium Costs of Health Insurance for Consumers) (govinfo)

title: United States military operation in Caracas; Nicolás Maduro taken into United States custody
whatHappened: On 3 January 2026 Nicolás Maduro Moros was placed in United States custody following a military operation in Caracas, Venezuela, and was transported to the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, New York, to await trial on Federal charges including narco-terrorism and drug trafficking. He had been indicted in the Southern District of New York in an indictment unsealed on 26 March 2020, and the Department of State increased its reward offer to up to $50 million.
whatItChanged: Removed a sitting head of state of another country by United States military action and placed him in United States criminal custody; a Senate resolution to limit military action in Venezuela failed on 14 January 2026, and Executive Order 14373 of 9 January 2026 addressed Venezuelan oil revenue.
sourceName: United States Department of State, Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs — Nicolás Maduro Moros (Captured)

title: Withdrawal directed from a schedule of international organisations, conventions and treaties
whatHappened: A Presidential Memorandum, acting on the review directed by Executive Order 14199 and on the Secretary of State's reported findings, directed withdrawal of the United States from a schedule of international intergovernmental organisations, conventions and treaties determined to be contrary to the interests of the United States, and directed the ending of associated funding and participation.
whatItChanged: Removed the United States from membership and funding in a defined set of multilateral bodies and instruments in a single instrument.
sourceName: The White House, Presidential Memorandum: Withdrawing the United States from International Organizations, Conventions, and Treaties that Are Contrary to the Interests of the United States

title: Two United States citizens fatally shot by Federal immigration agents in Minneapolis
whatHappened: A report by the minority staff of the House Committee on Oversight records that on 7 January 2026 Renée Nicole Macklin Good was fatally shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Minneapolis during Operation Metro Surge, and that on 24 January 2026 Alex Jeffrey Pretti was fatally shot by a Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer and agent less than two miles away. The report states the administration characterised the first shooting as self-defence and that recordings show the officer was not in the vehicle's path. NOTE: the source is a congressional committee minority-staff product that itself relies substantially on news reporting; no neutral executive-branch account of either shooting could be opened.
whatItChanged: Produced the deaths of two United States citizens at the hands of Federal immigration officers inside a major city during a Federal enforcement surge, and triggered the nationwide protest wave of January 2026.
sourceName: United States House of Representatives, Committee on Oversight (minority staff), report on Federal immigration enforcement in Minnesota

title: United States membership in the World Health Organization terminated
whatHappened: In a joint statement of 22 January 2026, the Secretary of State and the Secretary of Health and Human Services announced that 'Today, the United States withdrew from the World Health Organization (WHO)', completing the withdrawal begun by Executive Order 14155 of 20 January 2025 after the required one-year notice period.
whatItChanged: Ended United States membership, governance participation and funding in the World Health Organization.
sourceName: United States Department of State, Joint Statement by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. — Termination of U.S. Membership in the World Health Organization

title: Ice storm across the South and mid-Atlantic, 23-25 January 2026
whatHappened: The National Weather Service Jackson forecast office published an event summary for the 23-25 January 2026 ice storm. Emergency declarations were approved for a large group of Southern and mid-Atlantic States, and the National Weather Service Jackson area recorded eight deaths — five from cold exposure and three in fires linked to efforts to stay warm during power outages.
whatItChanged: Produced simultaneous multi-State emergency declarations and prolonged power loss across the South in the middle of the January 2026 political crisis.
sourceName: National Weather Service, Jackson, Mississippi — January 23-25, 2026 Ice Storm

title: Department of Justice published 3.5 million pages of Epstein records
whatHappened: The Department of Justice published over 3 million additional pages responsive to the Epstein Files Transparency Act, including more than 2,000 videos and 180,000 images, bringing the total production to nearly 3.5 million pages. The files were drawn from the Florida and New York cases against Jeffrey Epstein, the New York case against Ghislaine Maxwell, the cases investigating Epstein's death, multiple Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) investigations and the Office of Inspector General investigation into his death.
whatItChanged: Placed an entire Federal investigative file, including materials naming government officials, into the public record under statutory compulsion.
sourceName: United States Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs — Department of Justice Publishes 3.5 Million Responsive Pages in Compliance with the Epstein Files Transparency Act

title: Nationwide 'no work, no school, no shopping' strike against immigration enforcement
whatHappened: UNRESOLVED. Following the Minneapolis and Portland shootings, protests were reported across the United States from 7 January to 3 February 2026, including crowds reported at 50,000 to more than 100,000 in Minneapolis and a coordinated nationwide strike on 30 January 2026. No government statement, legislative research-service product, court ruling or official gazette attesting the strike or its scale could be opened; Department of Homeland Security releases located for the period concern arrests of protesters and threats against officers rather than the mobilisation itself. Pass A should seek a primary before any downstream pass relies on the scale figures.
whatItChanged: Not established from a primary source.
sourceName: UNRESOLVED — no primary source located

title: Second lapse in appropriations, 31 January to 3 February 2026
whatHappened: Office of Management and Budget Memorandum M-26-06 of 30 January 2026 notified agencies that appropriations for six of the bills carried in Division A of Public Law 119-37 — Defense, Financial Services and General Government, Homeland Security, Labor-Health and Human Services-Education, National Security and State, and Transportation-Housing and Urban Development — would expire at 11:59 p.m. that night and directed affected agencies to execute plans for an orderly shutdown. The lapse ended with enactment of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (Public Law 119-75) on 3 February 2026.
whatItChanged: Shut most of the government for a second time within three months and resolved all appropriations except a two-week extension for the Department of Homeland Security, which set up the third shutdown.
sourceName: Office of Management and Budget, Memorandum M-26-06, Status of Agency Operations (30 January 2026)

title: New START and its central limits expired
whatHappened: The Treaty between the United States of America and the Russian Federation on Measures for the Further Reduction and Limitation of Strategic Offensive Arms (New START) and its central limits expired on 5 February 2026. The treaty had been extended once, in 2021, for the maximum five years permitted and could not lawfully be extended again.
whatItChanged: Left the United States and the Russian Federation without any treaty limit on deployed strategic nuclear warheads and launchers, or the associated verification and inspection regime, for the first time since 1972.
sourceName: United States Department of State, New START Treaty

title: Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the 2009 greenhouse gas endangerment finding
whatHappened: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) finalised the rescission of the Administrator's 2009 findings of endangerment and cause or contribute for greenhouse gases under section 202(a) of the Clean Air Act, and repealed all greenhouse gas emission standards for light-, medium- and heavy-duty vehicles and engines for model years 2012 through 2027 and beyond. The rule was signed on 12 February 2026, published on 18 February 2026 and made effective 20 April 2026.
whatItChanged: Removed the legal predicate on which Federal greenhouse gas regulation of motor vehicles rested and repealed the standards built on it.
sourceName: Rescission of the Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding and Motor Vehicle Greenhouse Gas Emission Standards Under the Clean Air Act (Federal Register)

title: Seventy-five-day Department of Homeland Security shutdown, 14 February to 30 April 2026
whatHappened: Office of Management and Budget Memorandum M-26-08 of 13 February 2026 notified the Secretary of Homeland Security that appropriations provided through the Further Continuing Appropriations Act, 2026 (division H of Public Law 119-75) would expire at 11:59 p.m. that night and directed the Department to execute plans for an orderly shutdown. The memorandum records that the Administration had received approximately fifteen demands in ten subject areas from Democratic leadership on 4 February. The lapse ended on 30 April 2026 with enactment of the Homeland Security and Further Additional Continuing Appropriations Act, 2026 (Public Law 119-86).
whatItChanged: Left the department responsible for immigration enforcement, border control, aviation security and disaster response unfunded for seventy-five days — the longest partial shutdown on record — during the immigration-enforcement confrontation that caused it.
sourceName: Office of Management and Budget, Memorandum M-26-08, Status of Department of Homeland Security Operations (13 February 2026)

title: Supreme Court held that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorise tariffs
whatHappened: In Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, No. 24-1287, argued 5 November 2025 and decided 20 February 2026 (with No. 25-250, Trump v. V.O.S. Selections, Inc.), the Supreme Court held that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) does not authorise the President to impose tariffs. The Chief Justice wrote for the Court, which noted the Government's concession that the President enjoys no inherent authority to impose peacetime tariffs. The judgment in No. 24-1287 was vacated and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction; the judgment in No. 25-250 was affirmed.
whatItChanged: Invalidated the legal basis for the drug-trafficking and reciprocal tariffs imposed since February 2025 — the great majority of the tariff wall — and converted duties already collected under them into contested overpayments.
sourceName: Supreme Court of the United States, Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. 229 (2026) (slip opinion)

title: Temporary import surcharge imposed under section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 on the day the tariffs were struck down
whatHappened: On 20 February 2026 a Presidential Proclamation imposed a temporary import surcharge, invoking section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 (19 U.S.C. 2132), which empowers the President to act through surcharges and other special import restrictions to address fundamental international payments problems. The same day, Executive Order 14389 ended certain tariff actions and Executive Order 14388 continued the suspension of duty-free de minimis treatment for all countries.
whatItChanged: Substituted a different statutory authority for the tariffs invalidated hours earlier, keeping a broad import charge in place under a provision that carries its own rate and duration limits.
sourceName: Proclamation, Imposing a Temporary Import Surcharge To Address Fundamental International Payments Problems (Federal Register)

title: United States began hostilities against Iran — Operation Epic Fury
whatHappened: Hostilities between the United States and Iran began on 28 February 2026, as stated in an Executive Office of the President Statement of Administration Policy. The White House announced Operation Epic Fury as a military campaign to eliminate Iran's nuclear capability, destroy its ballistic missile arsenal, degrade its proxy networks and cripple its naval forces, executed in partnership with regional allies. No congressional authorisation for the use of military force against Iran was enacted; concurrent resolutions directing removal of forces were introduced in April, May and July 2026 and opposed by the Administration.
whatItChanged: Put the United States into a full interstate war, conducted under claimed Article II authority alone, with United States combat deaths in the region and strikes across Iranian territory.
sourceName: Executive Office of the President, Office of Management and Budget, Statement of Administration Policy on H. Con. Res. 86 (20 May 2026)

title: Executive order on citizenship verification and integrity in Federal elections
whatHappened: Executive Order 14399 directed measures on citizenship verification and integrity in Federal elections, addressed to Federal agencies and to the conduct of Federal elections.
whatItChanged: Asserted executive direction over aspects of Federal election administration, a function the Constitution assigns to the States and Congress, seven months before the November 2026 midterm elections.
sourceName: Executive Order 14399, Ensuring Citizenship Verification and Integrity in Federal Elections (Federal Register)

title: Ceasefire ordered in the Iran war
whatHappened: The President ordered a ceasefire that began on 7 April 2026, terminating the hostilities that had begun on 28 February 2026, as stated in Executive Office of the President Statements of Administration Policy of 20 May and 23 July 2026.
whatItChanged: Suspended active hostilities after roughly five and a half weeks of war and opened the negotiation that produced the June memorandum of understanding.
sourceName: Executive Office of the President, Office of Management and Budget, Statement of Administration Policy on H. Con. Res. 89 (23 July 2026)

title: Supreme Court held the Voting Rights Act did not require Louisiana's additional majority-minority district
whatHappened: In Louisiana v. Callais, No. 24-109, argued 24 March 2025, reargued 15 October 2025 and decided 29 April 2026 (with No. 24-110, Robinson v. Callais), the Supreme Court held that because the Voting Rights Act did not require Louisiana to create an additional majority-minority district, no compelling interest justified the race-based districting in the challenged map. The Court had ordered reargument to resolve whether compliance with the Voting Rights Act can supply a compelling reason for race-based districting, a question it had assumed for thirty years.
whatItChanged: Removed the assumption on which section 2 majority-minority districting had rested since the 1990s, with direct consequences for congressional maps in the States drawn under it.
sourceName: Supreme Court of the United States, Louisiana v. Callais, No. 24-109 (slip opinion, as revised 4 May 2026)

title: Schedule Policy/Career implemented in the excepted service
whatHappened: Executive Order 14410 directed implementation of Schedule Policy/Career in the excepted service, moving career Federal positions of a confidential, policy-determining, policy-making or policy-advocating character out of the competitive service.
whatItChanged: Removed competitive-service removal protections from a defined class of career civil service positions.
sourceName: Executive Order 14410, Implementing Schedule Policy/Career in the Excepted Service (Federal Register)

title: Secure America Act enacted by budget reconciliation
whatHappened: Public Law 119-98 (S. 2), enacted 10 June 2026 as reconciliation pursuant to title II of S. Con. Res. 33, appropriated additional funds to U.S. Customs and Border Protection and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including $9.55 billion available through fiscal year 2029 to hire, pay, train and equip Border Patrol agents and support personnel, plus further Department of Homeland Security appropriations under the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs and Judiciary titles.
whatItChanged: Locked multi-year immigration enforcement funding into law through the filibuster-proof reconciliation route, six weeks after the seventy-five-day shutdown fought over that enforcement.
sourceName: Public Law 119-98, Secure America Act (govinfo)

title: United States-Iran memorandum of understanding signed at Versailles
whatHappened: A memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Iran was signed on 17 June 2026. It requires the Government of the Islamic Republic of Iran to 'make arrangements using its best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels ... from the Persian Gulf to the Seas of Oman'.
whatItChanged: Formalised the April ceasefire in a written instrument covering navigation of the Strait of Hormuz; the Administration states Iran breached the navigation commitment within three weeks.
sourceName: Executive Office of the President, Office of Management and Budget, Statement of Administration Policy on H. Con. Res. 89 (23 July 2026)

title: Supreme Court decided the Temporary Protected Status termination cases
whatHappened: In Mullin, Secretary of Homeland Security v. Doe, No. 25-1083, argued 29 April 2026 and decided 25 June 2026 (with No. 25-1084, Trump v. Miot), the Supreme Court decided whether persons challenging the termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for nationals of Syria and Haiti were entitled to orders postponing the terminations during litigation. The Syrian designation, in place since 2012, was noticed for termination in September 2025 and the Haitian designation, in place since 2010, in November 2025.
whatItChanged: Resolved the interim-relief question governing whether long-standing Temporary Protected Status populations remain lawfully present while their terminations are litigated.
sourceName: Supreme Court of the United States, Mullin v. Doe, No. 25-1083 (slip opinion)

title: Supreme Court held the Federal Trade Commission's removal protection unconstitutional and overruled Humphrey's Executor
whatHappened: In Trump v. Slaughter, No. 25-332, argued 8 December 2025 and decided 29 June 2026, the Supreme Court held that the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) for-cause removal provision, 15 U.S.C. 41, is contrary to the separation of powers, and stated that 'If anything more is left of Humphrey's, we overrule it.' The case arose from the removal of Commissioners Rebecca Slaughter and Alvaro Bedoya in January 2025 without any statutory cause.
whatItChanged: Ended the ninety-one-year rule permitting Congress to insulate multi-member regulatory commissions from at-will presidential removal, placing the independent agencies under direct presidential control.
sourceName: Supreme Court of the United States, Trump v. Slaughter, No. 25-332 (slip opinion, as revised 7 July 2026)

title: Supreme Court denied the stay application in the attempted removal of a Federal Reserve Governor
whatHappened: In Trump v. Cook, No. 25A312, argued 21 January 2026 and decided 29 June 2026, the Supreme Court denied the Government's application to stay the preliminary injunction preventing the removal of Lisa Cook from the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. Cook was the first Governor the President had purported to fire in the central bank's 111-year history. The Court held the Government had not shown it was likely to prevail, and that accepting its position would transform the Federal Reserve's for-cause protection into at-will employment.
whatItChanged: Kept a contested Governor in office and preserved for-cause protection at the central bank in the same week the Court removed it at the other independent agencies.
sourceName: Supreme Court of the United States, Trump v. Cook, No. 25A312 (slip opinion)

title: Supreme Court held birthright citizenship extends to children of unlawfully or temporarily present parents
whatHappened: In Trump v. Barbara, No. 25-365, argued 1 April 2026 and decided 30 June 2026, the Supreme Court held that children born in the United States to parents unlawfully or temporarily present are 'subject to the jurisdiction' of the United States and are citizens at birth under the Citizenship Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The case challenged Executive Order 14160 of 20 January 2025, which had provided that such children do not qualify for citizenship.
whatItChanged: Struck down the executive attempt to narrow birthright citizenship and settled the constitutional question for children born to unlawfully or temporarily present parents.
sourceName: Supreme Court of the United States, Trump v. Barbara, No. 25-365 (slip opinion, as revised 1 July 2026)

title: Super Typhoon Bavi struck Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands
whatHappened: UNRESOLVED. Super Typhoon Bavi is reported to have passed through the Mariana Islands on about 6 July 2026 with wind gusts above 200 miles per hour, followed by emergency declarations for Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands on 3-4 July 2026 and a major disaster declaration for the Commonwealth announced on 4 August 2026. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) press releases and disaster records that carry these facts are served behind bot protection and returned HTTP 403 to every fetch attempted; no corresponding declaration notice has yet appeared in the Federal Register, and the National Weather Service Guam office publishes no retained storm summary. Pass A should re-attempt fema.gov by hand, or wait for the Federal Register declaration notice.
whatItChanged: Not established from a primary source.
sourceName: UNRESOLVED — primary sources (FEMA) not openable

title: United States strikes on Iran resumed after attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz
whatHappened: An Executive Office of the President Statement of Administration Policy of 23 July 2026 records that Iran attacked several neutral-flagged commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz from 6 July 2026, contrary to the June memorandum of understanding, and that at the President's direction United States Armed Forces responded 'commencing on July 7, 2026, with strikes against targets within Iran, including missile launch sites, air defenses, military maritime assets, military support infrastructure, and command and control capabilities'. The document states that United States forces 'continue to be engaged in operations' and that these are 'distinct and separate from prior operations'.
whatItChanged: Restarted the war three weeks after the memorandum of understanding was signed, under a new operational framing, with no congressional authorisation and with the Administration opposing the removal resolutions before Congress.
sourceName: Executive Office of the President, Office of Management and Budget, Statement of Administration Policy on H. Con. Res. 89 (23 July 2026)
